OneLake
Preview versions of Domains REST APIs are no longer available
We previously announced March 31, 2026, as the retirement date for the preview versions of Domains REST APIs. As a next step, we changed the default API behavior in August 2026. Requests that don't include the preview query parameter now use the Generally Available (GA) version instead of the preview version.
As of November 2026, the preview APIs have been removed completely. Any call that still explicitly requests the preview version will now fail. If your scripts, applications, or automation still use the preview APIs, update them to the GA API contract. Keep in mind that the GA contract includes breaking changes compared to the preview version.
This applies to the following APIs: Create Domain, Get Domain, List Domains, and Update Domain. Learn more about these APIs in the Domains REST API documentation.
Data Engineering
Access data with Power Query in Fabric notebooks (Preview)
Fabric notebooks now support running Power Query M queries through existing Fabric connections. Using the new notebookutils.powerquery capability, you can execute an M query and load the results directly into your notebook for further analysis.
Gateway-backed connections also enable notebooks to access supported on-premises data sources that are not directly accessible from Fabric compute.
The initial release supports read operations from supported data sources.
Figure: Power Query methods available through NotebookUtils in a Fabric notebook.
To learn more, refer to the Use Power Query with NotebookUtils in Fabric notebooks documentation.
Retrieve Fabric environment publishing logs through the public API (Preview)
The Fabric environment public API now supports retrieving publishing logs. You can use the API to access publishing results programmatically, monitor environment publishing in automated workflows, and investigate issues without relying solely on the Fabric user interface.
This capability helps teams integrate publishing-log retrieval into automated environment management and lifecycle processes.
To learn more, refer to the Retrieve publishing logs using the Fabric environment REST API documentation.
Use JFrog Artifactory with Fabric environment items (Preview)
Fabric environment items now support JFrog Artifactory as a package repository. Organizations can connect their existing JFrog repositories and use enterprise-managed packages when configuring libraries and dependencies for an environment.
This integration helps teams use their established package-management practices in Fabric while providing greater flexibility in how environment dependencies are sourced and managed.
Figure: Configuring a JFrog Artifactory connection for use with Fabric environment items.
To learn more, refer to the Manage Fabric environment libraries with JFrog Artifactory documentation.
Optimal refresh for deletes and updates in Materialized Lake Views (Preview)
Materialized Lake Views now extend optimal refresh beyond append-only data. With refresh hints, eligible views can process source deletes and updates incrementally, without recomputing the entire result.
For pipelines that remove expired records, update product details, or correct transactions, a small source change no longer must trigger a full recomputation solely because it includes deletes or updates.
Key benefits
• Process eligible deletes and updates incrementally.
• Reduce unnecessary full recomputations.
• Handle inserts, updates, and deletes together.
To use refresh hints, enable CDF on your source tables and add a REFRESH_HINT UNIQUE(...) clause to your Materialized Lake View definition. Specify a column, or combination of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in the view’s output.
Figure: Defining a refresh hint in the Materialized Lake View.
To learn more, refer to the Enable optimal refresh for deletes and updates in Materialized Lake Views (preview) documentation.
Broader SQL clause support for optimal refresh in Materialized Lake Views
Materialized Lake Views now support incremental refresh for a wider range of SQL clauses and operators. More existing queries can benefit from optimal refresh without being rewritten, processing eligible source changes rather than rebuilding the entire result. This reduces unnecessary full refreshes and compute use across more analytical workloads.
New clauses and expressions:
• RIGHT OUTER JOIN
• LEFT ANTI JOIN
• CROSS JOIN
• ORDER BY
To learn more, refer to the SQL constructs supported for optimal refresh documentation.
Email alerts for failures on Materialized Lake view runs
Know when a scheduled refresh fails, without watching for it.
Materialized Lake View refreshes often run in the background, and you shouldn’t have to continually check Recent runs to know when something needs attention. With email alerts for scheduled run failures, Fabric brings the failure to you so you can respond sooner.
When a scheduled refresh fails, the email includes error details and relevant run information, with a direct link to the failed run in Fabric, giving you the context to start investigating.
When configuring a time-based schedule, you can choose the Microsoft Entra users or groups who should receive these failure notifications.
Set the schedule, choose who should be notified, and let Fabric tell you when a Materialized lake view run need attention.
To learn more, refer to the Materialized Lake Views documentation.
File Data Ingestion with Materialized Lake Views in Microsoft Fabric (Preview)
File data ingestion with Materialized Lake Views (MLVs) in Microsoft Fabric is now available. Instead of building separate ingestion pipelines to move raw files into tables, you can ingest CSV and Parquet files directly from OneLake into a Materialized Lake View and make your bronze layer part of the same declarative pipeline as the rest of your medallion architecture.
Benefits of file data ingestion
Previously, you had to build and maintain a separate ingestion layer before you could get the benefits of MLVs, which had to start from tables. To get raw files into that first table, you'd reach for a shortcut transformation, a data pipeline, or a notebook load, which is a separate step to build and operate before your declarative pipeline could even begin.
File data ingestion removes that step. Point a Materialized Lake View at a folder of files, and Fabric handles the ingestion, materializes the results as a Delta table, and plugs it straight into the same lineage, scheduling, data quality, and monitoring that power the rest of your medallion architecture. One programming model, from raw files to gold.
A file-ingesting Materialized Lake View is defined with a USING OneLake_Files clause. You describe the source folder and format, and Fabric materializes it with end-to-end lineage visible to users.
Figure: Microsoft Fabric's lineage view connects a OneLake source folder to downstream materialized lake views. The Files processed pane shows the selected run's processed and skipped files, rows read and written, and diagnostic details.
To learn more, refer to the Spark SQL Reference for Materialized Lake Views documentation.
Data Warehouse
New Metadata Sync for SQL Analytics Endpoints with path to upgrade existing endpoints (Generally Available)
New metadata sync for SQL analytics endpoints is now generally available in Microsoft Fabric. We also introduce an on-demand upgrade path in preview for existing SQL analytics endpoints.
New metadata sync reduces the delay between lakehouse data availability and SQL queries. New architecture parses Delta logs, while optimized background processes handle data and schema changes separately. On-query refresh detects stale data and refreshes tables when you query them. Together, these improvements help make your data queryable in seconds, not minutes.
Key benefits
• Query newly available lakehouse data sooner.
• Handle data and schema changes independently.
• Read fresher data with on-query refresh.
• Assess existing endpoints before upgrading.
New endpoints use new metadata sync by default
New metadata sync is enabled by default for new workspaces. Newly created SQL analytics endpoints in existing workspaces also use the new architecture.
Manage this behavior under Workspace settings > Warehouse settings > New metadata sync. This setting does not upgrade existing endpoints.
Upgrade existing endpoints on demand (Preview)
The on-demand upgrade path lets you assess readiness and initiate an upgrade for an existing SQL analytics endpoint. Use the GetStatus API to check its current state. Run the Preflight API to identify tables that need attention. Address the findings, rerun Preflight, and invoke the Upgrade API. Track the long-running operation to completion, then validate endpoint status and table-level sync health.
For ongoing monitoring, use sys.dm_db_external_tables_log_status to inspect the latest sync time, process Delta log and checkpoint versions, and blocked status.
Figure: Enable new metadata sync for SQL analytics endpoints in Workspace settings.
To learn more, refer to the SQL analytics endpoint metadata sync and metadata sync monitoring DMV documentation.
Conversational Analytics
Improved datetime reasoning for Advanced NL2SQL (Preview)
Users often ask time-relative questions, such as "What were sales yesterday?" or "Show me last month's churn." To answer them correctly, the agent needs to know what "today" means for the person asking, and which time zone the data is stored in. In preview runtime, Advanced NL2SQL now handles both, so relative dates resolve consistently instead of depending on the server's clock.
What you get as a creator:
• Awareness of the current date and time. The agent picks up the user's time zone from the client, so "today," "last month," and "this year" resolve against the user's own calendar. A user in Seattle asking about "9 AM today" means 9 AM Pacific; a user in London means 9 AM London time.
• Time zone–aware queries. By default, the agent treats timestamp columns as UTC and converts the user's time to match before filtering, including daylight saving time adjustments.
• Control over how your data is stored. If a column uses a different time zone, declare it in the data source instructions (for example, "run_timestamp_dt is stored in Eastern Time"), and the agent converts to that zone when it generates SQL.
Datetime awareness is available today for SQL sources on the preview runtime. Switch your agent to the preview runtime to try it, and retest any instructions you previously wrote to work around date handling.
To learn more, refer to the Fabric data agent runtime documentation.
Add multiple topics for SQL sources in Data Agents (Preview)
Now, you can organize your Fabric data agent's SQL guidance into multiple topics instead of one long set of instructions. Upload existing markdown files or create new ones in the agent, with each file covering a specific business area, dataset, or type of question. When a user asks a question, the agent searches across your topics, picks the most relevant one, and pulls in only the parts of the instructions it needs to generate accurate SQL. Because topics are stored as markdown files and are part of Git integration, your team can version, review, and collaborate on them like the rest of your Fabric artifacts. This makes it easier to scale source-specific instructions as your data estate grows.
Figure: A lakehouse data source in a Fabric data agent with multiple SQL topics, each stored as its own markdown file.
To learn more, refer to the Use topics in a Fabric data agent (preview) documentation.
Query Templates for SQL and Semantic Models (Preview)
Query templates let you give your Fabric data agent ready-made queries for the questions your users ask most, for both SQL data sources and Power BI semantic models. A template is an example query that can be static or parameterized, so one template can answer many versions of a question, such as different regions, products, or time periods. You can create templates with Build with AI or with the context authoring skill.
When a question matches a template, the agent fills in the parameters and runs the query instead of writing one from scratch. That means faster responses, typically under 15 seconds, and more consistent answers. If a question doesn't match any template, the agent falls back to its standard NL2SQL or NL2DAX tools and uses your templates as example queries to ground the query it generates.
Figure: Creating a query template in a Fabric data agent. You add a static or parameterized example query that the agent can reuse to answer matching questions quickly and consistently.
To get started, refer to the Data Agent Example Queries documentation.
Advanced NL2SQL in Data Agents (Generally Available)
Advanced NL2SQL changes how the agent turns questions into SQL: instead of one-shot generation, the agent has sub-tools to explore schema, test joins, and look up real filter values before it writes SQL. It can follow your example queries by making approved modifications, such as literal filter or parameter substitutions. It can also ask targeted clarifying questions before generating SQL or explore the data to check its assumptions when no example applies.
You can inspect each step the agent took, and the assumptions and reasoning behind it. In internal benchmarks, smart-answer accuracy increased from 78.8% to 90.9%, and P95 latency dropped from 46.8 seconds to 32.9 seconds. Data agents on the standard runtime will get Advanced NL2SQL capabilities by default, with no opt-in required.
Figure: Animated GIF - Advanced NL2SQL in a Fabric data agent explores the schema, tests joins and looks up filter values before writing SQL, and each reasoning step is visible in the run.
To learn more, refer to the SQL sources in Fabric data agent documentation.
Advanced DAX in Data Agents (Generally Available)
Advanced DAX generation helps Fabric data agents answer complex questions over Power BI semantic models with greater accuracy. Rather than generating a query in a single pass, it uses multiple reasoning steps to inspect model metadata, resolve ambiguity, review intermediate results, and refine the query.
Instance value indexing helps match the terms in a user’s question to values stored in the model, producing more reliable filters even when the wording differs. By identifying relevant model objects and values more efficiently, advanced DAX generation can also reduce response latency.
Figure: Animated GIF - A Fabric data agent answers a sales question using instance value search to generate a more reliable DAX query with the right customer filters.
To learn more, refer to the advanced DAX generation and semantic model best practices documentation.
Configure Semantic Models in Data Agents (Preview)
Semantic models can now be configured directly within a data agent’s runtime. Add data source descriptions, instructions, and example queries, and fine-tune schema selection down to individual columns and measures. This allows you to configure everything in one place and tailor the same semantic model for different data agents, each with its own specialized configuration. You can also import existing AI schema selections and instructions from Prep Data for AI to reuse your existing configuration and get set up faster.
Figure: Animated GIF - A semantic model is added to a Fabric data agent, importing its existing configurations from Prep Data for AI, with additional configurations applied directly in the data agent.
To learn more, refer to the configuring semantic models in data agents documentation.
Build with AI Supports Topics
Build Agent with AI helps you create and refine topic-based instructions for your Data Agent. Explore existing topics, generate new topics for SQL and KQL data sources, and review proposed changes before saving them. Each generated topic includes a title, description, and instructional content, while run steps provide visibility into the changes and links to saved topics.
To learn more, refer to the Build agent with AI mode for data agent in Microsoft Fabric (preview) documentation.
Build with AI Supports Semantic Model Configurations
Build Agent with AI helps you configure Data Agent for Semantic Models by exploring tables, measures, and columns and using query history to inform instructions and example queries. Review generated configurations before applying changes, with run steps showing the queries used during exploration to help you understand how the recommendations were developed.
To learn more, refer to the Build agent with AI mode for data agent in Microsoft Fabric (preview) documentation.
Get user feedback for a Fabric data agent in Microsoft Copilot (Preview)
You can now review user feedback directly in the Fabric data agent interface, in addition to retrieving it through the existing data agent Python SDK. A Microsoft 365 administrator must first turn on “Agent feedback sharing” in the Microsoft 365 admin center. After you republish your agent to Microsoft Copilot, you can see the thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings users submit, along with their shared comments. Use this feedback to identify answers users found helpful and those that need work, then update your agent’s instructions, examples, or data sources.
Figure: Animated GIF - Monitor feedback from users for data agent from Microsoft Copilot.
To learn more, refer to the consumer creator feedback documentation.
Create a Rayfin App from Fabric data agent
The new Fabric data agent connector lets you connect a Rayfin app to your data agent. Rayfin provides tools for building and deploying apps on Microsoft Fabric. You can add the connector through the Rayfin command line and build an app where users ask questions and receive answers from your data agent.
Figure: Animated GIF - Create a Rayfin App from Fabric data agent.
To learn more, refer to the Create Rayfin App documentation.
Improved citation experience for Fabric data agent in Microsoft Copilot
Now, you can inspect how a Fabric data agent produced an answer in Microsoft Copilot. Select “View response details: Check what data was used and see step-by-step reasoning” to open the response in Fabric, where you can review the reasoning steps, data used, and query behind it. This gives users a way to check an answer and investigate results they did not expect.
Figure: Animated GIF - Improved citation experience for Fabric data agent in Microsoft Copilot to better understand how the answer was generated.
To learn more, refer to the Data Agent M365 documentation.
Observe Fabric data agent in Application Insight and Foundry Observability platform
You can now send logs and traces from your Fabric data agent to Azure Application Insights to monitor activity and investigate problems. Set up an Application Insights connection in Manage connections and gateways, then enable logging and tracing in your data agent. You can review the traces in Azure Monitor or Microsoft Foundry Observability. Two tenant settings control what is sent. Sharing operational details, such as agent and data source names, is on by default. Sharing user-level data, including prompts, responses, and generated queries, is off by default. Work with your Fabric administrator to enable the data you need and review where it will be stored and who can access it.
Figure: Animated GIF - Enable Agent Observability to access logs and traces for a Fabric data agent.
To learn more, refer to the Application Insights documentation.
Access the query as part of the traces for Fabric data agent in Microsoft Foundry
Traces for Fabric data agents used as tools in Microsoft Foundry can now include the query the data agent ran. Alongside the existing details about data sources, timing, and status, agent builders can inspect the query to check how data was retrieved and investigate incorrect or unexpected results.
To learn more, refer to the Data Agent Foundry documentation.
Semantic Model Topics
Semantic models will support long-form business guidance with Topics. Topics extend your model's measures, relationships, and definitions with instructions for interpreting and analyzing data. They are designed for AI consumption and interpretation across agents. Capture business expertise once and reuse it wherever people ask questions about that model through Fabric IQ.
Getting a useful answer often requires more than knowing which tables and measures to query. Your organization may have a specific definition of customer risk or a preferred approach to explaining changes in business performance. We heard your feedback that the space available for AI instructions in Prep for AI was too limited for this depth of guidance. Topics provide room for long-form instructions, including business rules, examples, recommended measures, and analytical procedures. Authors can organize that expertise into focused topics instead of compressing every scenario into a short set of general instructions.
Now, authoring is skill-based, without a dedicated topic authoring UI. Starting from a semantic model or Power BI report, work conversationally with the skill to draft and refine topics grounded in the available context. That shared context format helps agents identify relevant topics, interpret their instructions, and apply them when answering questions.
Topics complement Prep for AI. The work you've already done remains valuable, and existing AI instructions continue to be considered when answering questions about the model and are used as input for topic creation. Use those instructions for general guidance that persists across questions, and topics for detailed instructions selected when relevant. The distinction is about both depth and applicability. This preview is a step toward a more unified preparation experience, with expanded UI-based authoring planned in Fabric alongside skill-based workflows. We'll share more about bringing Prep for AI and model-level context together, preserving your investment and making guidance easier to manage.
Get started
To learn more about creating semantic model topics and get the skill from Skills for Fabric.
Fabric Capability in Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder (Generally Available)
Microsoft Fabric is now available as a capability in Microsoft 365 Copilot Agent Builder, allowing makers to create agents that answer business questions using data from Fabric.
Agent Builder provides a simple, natural-language experience for creating and customizing agents directly within Microsoft 365 Copilot, without requiring coding expertise.
By enabling the Fabric capability when configuring an agent, makers can bring existing Power BI reports and semantic models into their agent experiences without configuring individual data sources. Agents can discover relevant Fabric content and answer questions using the business data users already have access to, while respecting existing Fabric permissions and security controls.
This integration makes it easier to build agents grounded in trusted organizational data, bringing Fabric's analytical capabilities into customized Microsoft 365 Copilot experiences.
Figure: Animated GIF - Enabling the Fabric capability in Agent Builder and asking a business question using a Power BI report.
To learn more and get started, refer to the Use Fabric IQ in Microsoft 365 Agent Builder documentation.
Fabric data agents now return up to 1000 rows under standard runtime (Preview)
One of the most common requests we hear is about row limits. Previously, a Fabric data agent returned at most 25 rows with its answer, which is fine for a quick number but not enough when you want to see the whole result. Customers told us they want a full response so they can review it offline or run their own analysis on top of it. We previously lifted that limit in the preview runtime, and now this is enabled in the standard runtime. The response comes back as a summary followed by a tabular preview of up to 1000 rows.
This is the first step, and more is coming. Next, we plan to let you download the full response as an Excel file, with sensitivity labels carried through to the file. The experience is currently available only in the Fabric user interface and will soon be enabled across all integrations, including MCP endpoint, Microsoft Copilot Studio, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft Copilot. These improvements are landing over the next few months, so stay tuned.
Figure: Animated GIF - Fabric data agent to return up to 1000 rows under standard runtime.
To learn more, refer to the Data Agent File Support documentation.
Fabric data agents in Microsoft Copilot Chat (Generally Available)
With Fabric data agents available in Microsoft Copilot Chat, you can publish a data agent in Fabric and then add it to a conversation in Microsoft Copilot Chat to ask questions and get answers from your data. The experience is similar to adding a Word document to a chat. Instead of attaching a document, you add your published data agent.
To get started, open a chat and select Add content. You’ll find your data agent under the Fabric category. Select it to add it to the conversation, then ask your question. For example, if your agent is connected to sales data, you can ask how sales compare across locations and get an answer directly in the chat.
Figure: Animated GIF - Add a Fabric data agent to Microsoft Copilot Chat.
To learn more, refer to the data agent in Microsoft Copilot chat documentation.
Real-Time Intelligence
Smart Query Acceleration for Eventhouse (Preview)
Query acceleration for OneLake Shortcuts caches and indexes data as it lands in OneLake, providing performance comparable to ingesting data in Eventhouse. Smart Query Acceleration takes the guesswork out of tuning Query Acceleration by automatically adapting the Hot-cache period for external Delta tables as query patterns change. You can set MinHot and MaxHot as guardrails, defining the minimum and maximum amount of recent data Query Acceleration is allowed to keep accelerated, instead of manually choosing a fixed Hot period.
The feature continuously analyzes Eventhouse query activity and dynamically adjusts the Hot-cache period. Customers can select Performance mode to prioritize query speed or Cost mode to prioritize savings, with a potential performance trade-off.
For example, a 1–30-day adaptive range can be enabled with the following KQL command:
.alter external table MyExternalTable policy query_acceleration
'{"IsEnabled": true, "MinHot": "1.00:00:00", "MaxHot": "30.00:00:00", "Profile": "Performance"}'.
To learn more, refer to the Smart Query Acceleration documentation.
Create Activator alerts from Fabric Maps (Preview)
Fabric Maps help you understand what’s happening across locations, assets, and operational areas. Now, with integration with Fabric Activator, you can take the next step by turning those geospatial insights into proactive alerts and actions.
Instead of continuously monitoring a map for changes, you can define the conditions that matter to your business and let Activator monitor them for you. When those conditions are met, Activator can notify users or trigger automated actions, helping teams respond to important changes as they happen. For example, operations teams can monitor conditions across facilities or geographic areas and create alerts when key metrics cross defined thresholds. This makes it easier to move from seeing where something is happening on the map to acting when it matters.
Creating an alert starts directly from a supported layer in Fabric Maps. From the map experience, you can define what data to monitor, configure the condition you want to detect, and choose the appropriate action, bringing visualization, monitoring, and action together in a connected experience.
Figure: Animated GIF - Create Activator alerts from Fabric Maps to proactively monitor changing conditions.
With Fabric Maps and Activator working together, geospatial visualization becomes more than a way to explore your data. It becomes part of an operational workflow that helps you continuously monitor important conditions and respond faster when attention is needed.
To learn more, refer to the Activator alerts in Fabric Maps documentation.
What's new in Fabric Activator: More control and confidence (Generally Available)
Insight only matters if you act on it in time. Fabric Activator watches your streaming and event data across Microsoft Fabric and automatically sends an alert or starts an action when the conditions you set are met.
What’s new
• Generally Available: Activator alerts for Fabric Data Warehouse, with Private Link support.
• A new try sample experience: take Activator for a spin with live bike-station data. You'll watch real-time events stream in and set up alerts in minutes, replacing the old package-delivery sample.
• Take full control of your data flow: You can now start and stop ingestion on demand when you pause or delete your last rule.
Activator alerting for Data Warehouse (Generally Available)
You can set an Activator alert directly on the results of a T-SQL query in Fabric Data Warehouse. Use it to watch business KPIs, run data-quality checks, or track operational signals without building a separate monitoring pipeline.
Workspaces protected by private link can now use Activator alerts on Data Warehouse.
Get started
• Open your warehouse and run a query in the query editor.
• Select the Set alert entry point name.
• Set your condition, for example on each event or on each event when.
• Choose an action: email, Teams, or a Fabric item.
GIF IN SHAREPOINT
Figure: The following animation shows a query running in a warehouse, the Add rule pane opening, and a Teams message action being set up for the alert.
To learn more, refer to the Create an alert rule on a Fabric Warehouse SQL query documentation.
A new Try sample: explore Activator with live bike data
The Activator sample experience now uses real-time bike-rental data and replaces the package-delivery sample. Try the sample button in the same place. The scenario follows a bike rental company that monitors every station in real time and gets alerts when bikes run low or run out.
When you select Try sample and pick a workspace, Fabric provisions:
• An Eventstream using the built-in Bicycles sample source, published and already streaming.
• An Activator item connected to that stream.
• A bike station object model with properties such as bikes available, empty docks, and neighborhood.
• Five ready-made rules, created in a stopped state so nothing runs until you start them.
Figure: Select Try sample to start the bike-rental sample.
To learn more, refer to the Activator tutorial using sample data documentation.
Start and stop ingestion when no rules are running
When you stop or delete the last rule on a source, you can now stop ingestion in one step to free up capacity.
How it works
• When you stop or delete your last active rule on a source, a banner shows that data is still coming in.
• For KQL queries, SQL queries, Power BI metrics and Ontology sources, the banner links to Manage sources in Activator, or to Monitor if you're working inside a connected Fabric experience. From there, you can stop or start ingestion with one click.
• On the Manage source tab, set Status to Not ingesting to stop ingestion, or to Ingesting to resume.
• Creating a rule or restarting one on a stopped source also turns ingestion back on.
Should ingestion stay on or be turned off?
Keeping ingestion on keeps your charts current, preserves your data history, and lets rules restart without waiting for data to catch up. When no rules are running, ingestion still uses capacity, so stop it to free up capacity units (CUs).
GIF IN SHAREPOINT
Figure: The following animation shows the banner that appears after the last rule stops, and the Manage source tab where you switch the source to Not ingesting.
To learn more, refer to the Activator ingestion overview documentation.
Share your feedback
We'd like to hear your feedback and ideas. Join the discussion in the Activator community
App development
Fabric Apps and Rayfin (Generally Available)
Building business applications just got easier. Fabric apps in Microsoft and Rayfin make it possible for developers and AI agents to build and deploy complete applications with enterprise data, security, and governance built in. Rayfin brings together databases, authentication, backend functions, storage, and observability in one platform, eliminating the need to assemble and manage a separate backend stack. With direct access to existing Fabric data, including semantic models, warehouses, and lakehouses, teams can turn trusted business data into applications faster.
Support for new features including storage and Postgres
Fabric apps now support OneLake storage, allowing builders to store and serve images, documents, and other files alongside their relational data. We’re also introducing PostgreSQL support through Fabric HorizonDB, our new serverless PostgreSQL offering, giving builders the flexibility to choose between SQL and PostgreSQL.
Build Fabric-backed applications directly in Microsoft Copilot
Users can describe the app they need in natural language directly in Microsoft Copilot. When the app needs more advanced capabilities, Microsoft Fabric can provide the database and backend services through the integration with Copilot Managed Runtime, so an app that starts as a conversation can grow to store data, run business logic, and support more sophisticated scenarios
Expanded app-building experiences with Power BI
We’re expanding Fabric apps to Power BI Pro, enabling more Power BI users to build interactive applications on their existing data. Power BI Desktop for apps let users turn existing semantic models into interactive apps that run on Microsoft Fabric, making it easier to build on trusted Power BI data and move from insights to applications that support business workflows and action.
To learn more, refer to the Build enterprise apps faster with Rayfin documentation.
New centralized app governance in OneLake Governance hub
As more teams build applications with AI, organizations need greater visibility and control over what gets deployed. The new Apps view in the OneLake Governance hub gives Fabric administrators a centralized way to observe applications across their organization and block or unblock them when needed.
Figure: New App management page in OneLake Governance hub.
New security controls give administrators more flexibility to manage how applications access external resources and where they can run:
• Content Security Policy (CSP): Lets administrators restrict which external resources an application can load in the browser.
• Secure Embed: Lets administrators require that applications run within an embedded frame.
To learn more, refer to the Fabric apps governance documentation.
Support for new features including storage and PostgreSQL
Apps in Fabric and Rayfin now support OneLake storage, allowing builders to store and serve images, documents, and other files alongside their relational data. We’re also introducing PostgreSQL support through HorizonDB in Fabric, our new serverless PostgreSQL offering, giving builders the flexibility to choose between MSSQL and PostgreSQL.
Figure: New Fabric Apps storage page.
To learn more, refer to the Fabric Apps Storage, and Fabric Apps documentation.
Build Fabric-backed applications directly in Microsoft Copilot
With Rayfin integrated into Microsoft Copilot, users can now build applications using natural language, right from the familiar Copilot experience. Rayfin provides the underlying database and backend services, making app creation accessible to business users and turning conversations into working applications.
To learn more, refer to the Fabric apps in Copilotdocumentation.
Expanded app-building experiences with Power BI
We're expanding access to Rayfin through Power BI Pro, enabling more Power BI users to build applications. We're also introducing modern report apps in Power BI Desktop, allowing users to turn their existing semantic models into interactive, data-rich applications powered by Rayfin. Together, these capabilities make it easier for organizations to build on their Power BI investments and move beyond insights to applications that drive business workflows and action.
Figure: New app building experience in Power BI Desktop app.
To learn more, refer to the Fabric Apps Blog Report documentation.
Databases
Fabric HorizonDB
Build intelligent PostgreSQL applications with Microsoft Fabric HorizonDB
Fabric HorizonDB is a new serverless, Fabric-native PostgreSQL database designed for modern data and AI applications. It brings the power and familiarity of PostgreSQL directly into Microsoft Fabric, enabling developers to build transactional applications alongside Fabric's analytics, data engineering, and AI capabilities.
With Fabric HorizonDB, developers can create and manage PostgreSQL databases directly within their Fabric workspaces, using familiar PostgreSQL tools, drivers, and SQL. Its fully managed, serverless architecture simplifies database operations with automatic pause and resume, allowing teams to focus on building applications rather than managing infrastructure.
What makes Fabric HorizonDB particularly powerful is its native integration with the broader Fabric data ecosystem. Traditionally, operational databases and analytical platforms have operated as separate systems, requiring complex data pipelines, duplication, and synchronization to connect application data with business insights. Fabric HorizonDB helps bridge this gap, bringing operational and analytical workloads closer together within a unified platform.
Connect operational and analytical data with Federated Analytics
Fabric HorizonDB introduces Federated Analytics, a set of capabilities that enables developers to connect PostgreSQL transactional data with analytical data across Microsoft Fabric.
Federated Analytics supports three complementary integration patterns:
• Mirror operational data into Fabric: Make transactional data from Fabric HorizonDB available in OneLake for downstream analytics, reporting, and AI workloads, without building and maintaining traditional ETL pipelines.
• Query Fabric data directly from PostgreSQL: Use familiar SQL to access analytical data stored in Fabric warehouses and lakehouses, combining operational and analytical information in queries without first copying the analytical data into PostgreSQL.
• Bring analytical insights back into applications: Load curated datasets and analytical results from Fabric into HorizonDB, making them available to operational applications that need to act on business insights.
Together, these capabilities enable a more connected approach to building applications, where operational data can inform analytics and analytical insights can flow back into transactional experiences.
Figure: Fabric HorizonDB unifies operational and analytical data through a single PostgreSQL endpoint, enabling applications to query, analyze, and act on data across Fabric and OneLake.
For example, a retail application could combine live customer orders stored in PostgreSQL with historical purchasing trends and customer segmentation data from Fabric. Developers could use these insights to deliver personalized recommendations, improve customer experiences, or power intelligent application workflows—all while maintaining PostgreSQL as the operational database.
A native PostgreSQL experience, integrated into Fabric
Fabric HorizonDB also provides a streamlined developer experience that makes it easier to get started.
Developers can create a HorizonDB database directly from the New item experience in a Fabric workspace, connect using standard PostgreSQL clients, and begin building applications using familiar development tools.
The database becomes part of the Fabric environment, providing a natural connection between operational applications and the data, analytics, and AI capabilities already available to Fabric users.
Fabric HorizonDB in action
Figure: Animated GIF -Creating a Fabric HorizonDB database directly from the Microsoft Fabric workspace using the new item experience.
Fabric HorizonDB also serves as a PostgreSQL database option for Fabric apps, giving developers an operational data foundation for building data-driven applications within Fabric.
By combining PostgreSQL with Fabric's analytical capabilities, developers can build applications that go beyond traditional transactional processing—incorporating historical insights, analytical context, and AI-powered experiences into everyday business workflows.
From data to insights to action
Fabric HorizonDB represents an important step toward bringing operational databases, analytics, and AI together.
Instead of treating transactional applications and analytical systems as disconnected environments, developers can work with operational and analytical data through complementary integration patterns, choosing when to mirror, query remotely, or load data based on application requirements.
The result is a more connected foundation for building intelligent applications—where PostgreSQL powers transactions, Fabric delivers analytical insights, and applications can turn those insights into meaningful actions.
To learn more, refer to the Explore Microsoft Fabric documentation.
Data Factory
New Copilot experience in Dataflow Gen2 (Preview)
The new Copilot experience in Dataflow Gen2 helps you work through data preparation tasks in a conversation—from finding data to exploring the results. In Microsoft Fabric Data Factory, describe the outcome you need, review Copilot’s progress, and refine the result with follow-up requests. Your queries and Power Query M code remain available in the editor to inspect and adjust.
With the new experience, you can:
• Find and connect to data: Discover existing connections you can access, reference queries, and add files through supported import options.
• Build and reshape queries: Ask Copilot to combine data, filter rows, add transformations, or create a summary query.
• Understand and explore results: Get explanations of queries and selected steps, inspect inline data previews, and visualize results with charts.
• Investigate refresh and performance issues: Explore query folding and use available refresh history and diagnostics to investigate failures.
• Prepare your output: Configure data destinations and, where supported, ask Copilot to save and run the dataflow with your confirmation.
Figure: Start a conversation with Copilot alongside the Power Query editor.
Start with a request such as “Create a query that summarizes Orders by month and show a chart.” Then follow up with “Show a preview of the summary” or “Explain the steps you added.” You can refine the query and explore its results within the same conversation.
To try it, open a Dataflow Gen2 and select Copilot on the Home tab.
Figure: Inspect query results directly in the Copilot conversation.Figure: Explore query results through charts in the Copilot conversation.
Copilot asks for approval by default before replacing or deleting existing query content. Each save-and-run request requires confirmation. To return to the legacy experience, use the toggle at the top right of the Copilot pane when no response is active.
To learn more and get started, refer to Copilot in Dataflow Gen2 and Copilot capabilities in Dataflow Gen2.
Browse SharePoint files and folders in Dataflow Gen2 (Preview)
Find the SharePoint data you need without leaving Dataflow Gen2 or copying site and file URLs. The new SharePoint browser in Get data lets you explore sites you can access, navigate folders, and choose whether to connect to one file or work with a folder’s files.
Use the browser to:
• Find your starting point: Browse accessible sites, follow the breadcrumb through folders, search within the current location, and refresh the displayed items.
• Connect to the right files: Select one file or a folder, or leave items unselected to create a query listing files at your current location. Use filters to narrow the displayed list.
• Control what you include: Select Exclude subfolders when you want only the current folder’s files, then use Power Query to filter or combine the file list.
For example, browse to a folder of monthly sales files, bring its file list into the editor, and use Combine files to prepare one table for analysis. You can also connect to a single workbook when you only need that file.
To try it, open a Dataflow Gen2, select Get data on the Home tab, and choose SharePoint.
Figure: Browse SharePoint folders and choose files directly from Get data.
Learn more about How to combine files in Power Query in the documentation.
New Browse Azure experience in Dataflow Gen2 (Preview)
The new Browse Azure experience in Dataflow Gen2 makes it easier to find and connect to Azure-hosted data. It replaces the previous subscription and resource-group selection flow with a flat resource list, contextual filters, and breadcrumb navigation—so you can start with the resource information you know rather than work through a fixed hierarchy.
Previously, you used subscription and resource-group selectors to narrow the resources shown. The new browser displays resource groups alongside other items and exposes fields such as Subscription ID, Resource group, Type, and Location. This helps you distinguish similarly named resources and find the right starting point without first navigating through each level.
Figure: Find Azure resources in a flat list with contextual information.
Use Search to find items at your current location or combine filters to narrow the list. For example, filter by subscription and resource group to locate the storage account used by your analytics team. As you browse further, the columns and available filters adapt to the items at that location.
Figure: Narrow the resource list using contextual filters, including Subscription ID.
The experience follows the same browsing pattern as the new SharePoint browser. Double-click a navigable item or use its navigation arrow to explore its contents, follow the breadcrumb to return to an earlier location, and refresh the displayed items when needed. That consistency makes moving between Azure and SharePoint more familiar, while each browser retains controls appropriate to its source.
For Azure, opening a resource reveals the connection options or contents relevant to that resource. A storage account can offer storage connector choices, while a database server can expose databases to select. Unlike SharePoint browsing, Azure doesn’t provide an Exclude subfolders checkbox.
Figure: Navigate into a storage account and choose an available connection option.
The next experience also reflects the data you select. A JSON file can open a table preview, while an Excel workbook can open a Navigator where you choose the sheets, tables, or other workbook items you want to connect to.
To try the new browser, open a Dataflow Gen2, select Get data on the Home tab, and choose Azure
Google BigQuery data destination and Amazon S3 connectivity in Dataflow Gen2 (Preview)
Many organizations work across more than one cloud. One team might analyze data in Google BigQuery, while another relies on files in Amazon S3 to support an existing application. Dataflow Gen2 adds both platforms as data destinations, giving you more choice about where your prepared data goes.
You can use the familiar Power Query experience in Microsoft Fabric to connect to your sources, clean up data, and combine information from different systems. Once the data is ready, write the results to tables in Google BigQuery or files in Amazon S3. This brings cross-cloud delivery into the same low-code workflow you use for data preparation.
Amazon S3 is also available as a data source in Dataflow Gen2. You can read files from your S3 buckets, combine that data with information from other systems, and transform it using Power Query before loading the results to a supported destination. This means S3 can be both the starting point and the destination for your data preparation workflow.
Figure: Configure an Amazon S3 source connection in Dataflow Gen2.
For example, you might consolidate sales data from several regions into a dataset for a finance team working in BigQuery. Or you might prepare a cleaned file for a downstream process that reads from an S3 bucket. In either case, you can choose the destination that fits how the data will be used, rather than building your preparation workflow around where it needs to land.
Figure: Choose Google BigQuery or Amazon S3 as a data destination in Dataflow Gen2.
To learn more, refer to the Dataflow Gen2 data destinations documentation.
HTML document builder and Send Email with HTML bodies in Dataflow Gen2 (Preview)
Dataflow Gen2 is adding more ways to share the results of your data preparation, beyond delivering rows and columns to a destination. With the HTML document builder, you can turn prepared data into formatted HTML documents through a visual authoring experience.
Think of a weekly business update: you have already brought the data together and applied the transformations, but your audience needs a readable summary rather than another dataset to explore. The HTML document builder helps you present those results with context. You might create a sales summary for regional managers or an operational update that brings the most relevant information together in one document.
Alongside HTML document authoring, the Send Email action gains support for HTML message bodies. Using an Outlook connection, you can send formatted messages as part of a dataflow refresh instead of relying only on plain text. This gives you more control over how an update is presented in the recipient’s inbox, making it easier to scan and understand.
Figure: Configure a chart in the HTML document builder in Dataflow Gen2.
Learn more about the HTML document builder in Dataflow Gen2, and sending email from Dataflow Gen2.
PostgreSQL data destination in Dataflow Gen2 (Generally Available)
For teams that already use PostgreSQL, getting prepared data into the database is an important part of the workflow. The PostgreSQL data destination in Dataflow Gen2 lets you combine and transform data with Power Query, then load the results directly into the database your applications and reporting solutions already use.
Consider a team that brings together information from several business systems. Before that data is useful, they need to standardize column names, correct data types, and apply business calculations. With Dataflow Gen2, those steps can live in one data preparation workflow, with PostgreSQL as the destination for the resulting dataset. The applications consuming that table can work with the prepared results rather than repeating the same cleanup.
Configuration follows the familiar data destination experience: connect to your PostgreSQL database, select a destination table, and configure the column mapping. Each dataflow refresh writes the transformed query results to PostgreSQL, keeping preparation and delivery together and reducing the need for a separate export process.
Figure: Select PostgreSQL database as a data destination in Dataflow Gen2.
To learn more, refer to the PostgreSQL connector documentation.
Upgrade Power BI Dataflows Gen1 to Dataflow Gen2 (CI/CD) with the Upgrade Wizard and API (Generally Available)
The Dataflows Upgrade Wizard and the Upgrade API for Power BI Dataflows Gen1 to Dataflow Gen2 (CI/CD) are now Generally Available, so you can use them for your production upgrades. The wizard is a guided, end-to-end experience that upgrades a single dataflow, or several dataflows from a workspace, in a single flow. The API lets you assess readiness and upgrade dataflows in bulk, so you can automate upgrades across your workspaces.
New in this release:
• Upgrade dataflows you don't own: Users with the Admin workspace role and Tenant Admins can now upgrade dataflows owned by others directly in the wizard. The original owner and supported data source connections are kept, so there's no ownership transfer or connection setup to redo.
• Detect unresolved data source connections: The assessment now flags data source connections that aren't resolved, so you can fix them before you upgrade.
Figure: The assessment flags dataflows with unresolved data source connections before you upgrade.
To learn more, refer to the Upgrade Dataflow Gen1 to Dataflow Gen2 (CI/CD) using the Upgrade Wizard and the Upgrade API documentation.
Mapping Data Flow Transforms in Dataflow Gen2 (Generally Available)
Mapping Data Flow (MDF) Transforms in Dataflow Gen2 can be used for your production transformation workloads in Microsoft Fabric. Build visual, Spark-scale transformations without writing code, or bring existing Mapping Data Flows from Azure Data Factory and Azure Synapse Analytics into Fabric while retaining your transformation logic.
Figure: Visually author and preview Spark-scale transformations with MDF Transforms in Dataflow Gen2.
To learn more, refer to the Mapping Data Flow Transforms in Dataflow Gen2 and the Upgrade Azure Data Factory pipelines with Mapping Data Flows to Fabric documentation.
Bring Viva Insights data to your analytics platform (Preview)
Copy job and Viva Insights now provide a scheduled, governed way to export Copilot and workplace analytics data into your analytics platform. Organizations measuring the impact of Microsoft 365 Copilot bring adoption and usage data together with HR attributes, license spend, survey results and data from other AI tools, and report on it in the platforms their leadership already uses. Copy job in Microsoft Fabric delivers Viva Insights data to those platforms as a scheduled, fully managed export.
Figure: The new Viva Insights connector in Copy job.
You choose the Viva Insights datasets you want and the destination they should land in. Microsoft maintains the connector, keeps the schema in step, runs the job on your schedule and recovers failures, so no one on your team must maintain a pipeline.
For more information, refer to the Viva Insights documentation.
That’s a wrap!
From new data agent capabilities and AI-assisted app development to improvements across data engineering, real-time intelligence, and data preparation, this month’s updates give you more ways to work with your data and turn insights into action.
There will not be a December feature summary, but we’ll be back in the new year with more updates from Microsoft Fabric. Until then, explore the features that are most relevant to your work, refer to the linked documentation to learn more, and let us know what you think.
Check out the Fabric November Monthly Update Video for demos, and more information about this month's updates.

OneLake

Preview versions of Domains REST APIs are no longer available

We previously announced March 31, 2026, as the retirement date for the preview versions of Domains REST APIs. As a next step, we changed the default API behavior in August 2026. Requests that don't include the preview query parameter now use the Generally Available (GA) version instead of the preview version.

As of November 2026, the preview APIs have been removed completely. Any call that still explicitly requests the preview version will now fail. If your scripts, applications, or automation still use the preview APIs, update them to the GA API contract. Keep in mind that the GA contract includes breaking changes compared to the preview version.

This applies to the following APIs: Create Domain, Get Domain, List Domains, and Update Domain. Learn more about these APIs in the Domains REST API documentation.

Data Engineering

Access data with Power Query in Fabric notebooks (Preview)

Fabric notebooks now support running Power Query M queries through existing Fabric connections. Using the new notebookutils.powerquery capability, you can execute an M query and load the results directly into your notebook for further analysis.

Gateway-backed connections also enable notebooks to access supported on-premises data sources that are not directly accessible from Fabric compute.

The initial release supports read operations from supported data sources.

Figure: Power Query methods available through NotebookUtils in a Fabric notebook.

To learn more, refer to the Use Power Query with NotebookUtils in Fabric notebooks documentation.

Retrieve Fabric environment publishing logs through the public API (Preview)

The Fabric environment public API now supports retrieving publishing logs. You can use the API to access publishing results programmatically, monitor environment publishing in automated workflows, and investigate issues without relying solely on the Fabric user interface.

This capability helps teams integrate publishing-log retrieval into automated environment management and lifecycle processes.

To learn more, refer to the Retrieve publishing logs using the Fabric environment REST API documentation.

Use JFrog Artifactory with Fabric environment items (Preview)

Fabric environment items now support JFrog Artifactory as a package repository. Organizations can connect their existing JFrog repositories and use enterprise-managed packages when configuring libraries and dependencies for an environment.

This integration helps teams use their established package-management practices in Fabric while providing greater flexibility in how environment dependencies are sourced and managed.

Figure: Configuring a JFrog Artifactory connection for use with Fabric environment items.

To learn more, refer to the Manage Fabric environment libraries with JFrog Artifactory documentation.

Optimal refresh for deletes and updates in Materialized Lake Views (Preview)

Materialized Lake Views now extend optimal refresh beyond append-only data. With refresh hints, eligible views can process source deletes and updates incrementally, without recomputing the entire result.

For pipelines that remove expired records, update product details, or correct transactions, a small source change no longer must trigger a full recomputation solely because it includes deletes or updates.

Key benefits

  • Process eligible deletes and updates incrementally.
  • Reduce unnecessary full recomputations.
  • Handle inserts, updates, and deletes together.

To use refresh hints, enable CDF on your source tables and add a REFRESH_HINT UNIQUE(...) clause to your Materialized Lake View definition. Specify a column, or combination of columns, that uniquely identifies each row in the view’s output.

Figure: Defining a refresh hint in the Materialized Lake View.

To learn more, refer to the Enable optimal refresh for deletes and updates in Materialized Lake Views (preview) documentation.

Broader SQL clause support for optimal refresh in Materialized Lake Views

Materialized Lake Views now support incremental refresh for a wider range of SQL clauses and operators. More existing queries can benefit from optimal refresh without being rewritten, processing eligible source changes rather than rebuilding the entire result. This reduces unnecessary full refreshes and compute use across more analytical workloads.

New clauses and expressions:

  • RIGHT OUTER JOIN 
  • LEFT ANTI JOIN 
  • CROSS JOIN
  • ORDER BY

To learn more, refer to the SQL constructs supported for optimal refresh documentation.

Email alerts for failures on Materialized Lake view runs

Know when a scheduled refresh fails, without watching for it.

Materialized Lake View refreshes often run in the background, and you shouldn’t have to continually check Recent runs to know when something needs attention. With email alerts for scheduled run failures, Fabric brings the failure to you so you can respond sooner.

When a scheduled refresh fails, the email includes error details and relevant run information, with a direct link to the failed run in Fabric, giving you the context to start investigating.

When configuring a time-based schedule, you can choose the Microsoft Entra users or groups who should receive these failure notifications.

Set the schedule, choose who should be notified, and let Fabric tell you when a Materialized lake view run need attention.

To learn more, refer to the Materialized Lake Views documentation.

File Data Ingestion with Materialized Lake Views in Microsoft Fabric (Preview)

File data ingestion with Materialized Lake Views (MLVs) in Microsoft Fabric is now available. Instead of building separate ingestion pipelines to move raw files into tables, you can ingest CSV and Parquet files directly from OneLake into a Materialized Lake View and make your bronze layer part of the same declarative pipeline as the rest of your medallion architecture.

Benefits of file data ingestion

Previously, you had to build and maintain a separate ingestion layer before you could get the benefits of MLVs, which had to start from tables. To get raw files into that first table, you'd reach for a shortcut transformation, a data pipeline, or a notebook load, which is a separate step to build and operate before your declarative pipeline could even begin.

File data ingestion removes that step. Point a Materialized Lake View at a folder of files, and Fabric handles the ingestion, materializes the results as a Delta table, and plugs it straight into the same lineage, scheduling, data quality, and monitoring that power the rest of your medallion architecture. One programming model, from raw files to gold.

A file-ingesting Materialized Lake View is defined with a USING OneLake_Files clause. You describe the source folder and format, and Fabric materializes it with end-to-end lineage visible to users.

Figure: Microsoft Fabric's lineage view connects a OneLake source folder to downstream materialized lake views. The Files processed pane shows the selected run's processed and skipped files, rows read and written, and diagnostic details.

To learn more, refer to the Spark SQL Reference for Materialized Lake Views documentation.

Data Warehouse

New Metadata Sync for SQL Analytics Endpoints with path to upgrade existing endpoints (Generally Available)

New metadata sync for SQL analytics endpoints is now generally available in Microsoft Fabric. We also introduce an on-demand upgrade path in preview for existing SQL analytics endpoints.

New metadata sync reduces the delay between lakehouse data availability and SQL queries. New architecture parses Delta logs, while optimized background processes handle data and schema changes separately. On-query refresh detects stale data and refreshes tables when you query them. Together, these improvements help make your data queryable in seconds, not minutes.

Key benefits

  • Query newly available lakehouse data sooner.
  • Handle data and schema changes independently.
  • Read fresher data with on-query refresh.
  • Assess existing endpoints before upgrading.

New endpoints use new metadata sync by default

New metadata sync is enabled by default for new workspaces. Newly created SQL analytics endpoints in existing workspaces also use the new architecture.

Manage this behavior under Workspace settings > Warehouse settings > New metadata sync. This setting does not upgrade existing endpoints.

Upgrade existing endpoints on demand (Preview)

The on-demand upgrade path lets you assess readiness and initiate an upgrade for an existing SQL analytics endpoint. Use the GetStatus API to check its current state. Run the Preflight API to identify tables that need attention. Address the findings, rerun Preflight, and invoke the Upgrade API. Track the long-running operation to completion, then validate endpoint status and table-level sync health.

For ongoing monitoring, use sys.dm_db_external_tables_log_status to inspect the latest sync time, process Delta log and checkpoint versions, and blocked status.

Figure: Enable new metadata sync for SQL analytics endpoints in Workspace settings.

To learn more, refer to the SQL analytics endpoint metadata sync and metadata sync monitoring DMV documentation.

Conversational Analytics

Improved datetime reasoning for Advanced NL2SQL (Preview)

Users often ask time-relative questions, such as "What were sales yesterday?" or "Show me last month's churn." To answer them correctly, the agent needs to know what "today" means for the person asking, and which time zone the data is stored in. In preview runtime, Advanced NL2SQL now handles both, so relative dates resolve consistently instead of depending on the server's clock.

What you get as a creator:

  • Awareness of the current date and time. The agent picks up the user's time zone from the client, so "today," "last month," and "this year" resolve against the user's own calendar. A user in Seattle asking about "9 AM today" means 9 AM Pacific; a user in London means 9 AM London time.
  • Time zone–aware queries. By default, the agent treats timestamp columns as UTC and converts the user's time to match before filtering, including daylight saving time adjustments.
  • Control over how your data is stored. If a column uses a different time zone, declare it in the data source instructions (for example, "run_timestamp_dt is stored in Eastern Time"), and the agent converts to that zone when it generates SQL.

Datetime awareness is available today for SQL sources on the preview runtime. Switch your agent to the preview runtime to try it, and retest any instructions you previously wrote to work around date handling.

What makes Fabric HorizonDB particularly powerful is its native integration with the broader Fabric data ecosystem. Traditionally, operational databases and analytical platforms have operated as separate systems, requiring complex data pipelines, duplication, and synchronization to connect application data with business insights. Federated Analytics supports three complementary integration patterns:

  • Mirror operational data into Fabric: Make transactional data from Fabric HorizonDB available in OneLake for downstream analytics, reporting, and AI workloads, without building and maintaining traditional ETL pipelines.
  • Query Fabric data directly from PostgreSQL: Use familiar SQL to access analytical data stored in Fabric warehouses and lakehouses, combining operational and analytical information in queries without first copying the analytical data into PostgreSQL.
  • Bring analytical insights back into applications: Load curated datasets and analytical results from Fabric into HorizonDB, making them available to operational applications that need to act on business insights.

Together, these capabilities enable a more connected approach to building applications, where operational data can inform analytics and analytical insights can flow back into transactional experiences.

HTML document builder and Send Email with HTML bodies in Dataflow Gen2 (Preview)

Dataflow Gen2 is adding more ways to share the results of your data preparation, beyond delivering rows and columns to a destination. With the HTML document builder, you can turn prepared data into formatted HTML documents through a visual authoring experience.

Think of a weekly business update: you have already brought the data together and applied the transformations, but your audience needs a readable summary rather than another dataset to explore. The HTML document builder helps you present those results with context. You might create a sales summary for regional managers or an operational update that brings the most relevant information together in one document.

Alongside HTML document authoring, the Send Email action gains support for HTML message bodies. Using an Outlook connection, you can send formatted messages as part of a dataflow refresh instead of relying only on plain text. This gives you more control over how an update is presented in the recipient’s inbox, making it easier to scan and understand.

Figure: Configure a chart in the HTML document builder in Dataflow Gen2.

Learn more about the HTML document builder in Dataflow Gen2, and sending email from Dataflow Gen2.

PostgreSQL data destination in Dataflow Gen2 (Generally Available)

For teams that already use PostgreSQL, getting prepared data into the database is an important part of the workflow. The PostgreSQL data destination in Dataflow Gen2 lets you combine and transform data with Power Query, then load the results directly into the database your applications and reporting solutions already use.

Consider a team that brings together information from several business systems. Before that data is useful, they need to standardize column names, correct data types, and apply business calculations. With Dataflow Gen2, those steps can live in one data preparation workflow, with PostgreSQL as the destination for the resulting dataset. The applications consuming that table can work with the prepared results rather than repeating the same cleanup.

Configuration follows the familiar data destination experience: connect to your PostgreSQL database, select a destination table, and configure the column mapping. Each dataflow refresh writes the transformed query results to PostgreSQL, keeping preparation and delivery together and reducing the need for a separate export process.

Figure: Select PostgreSQL database as a data destination in Dataflow Gen2.

To learn more, refer to the PostgreSQL connector documentation.

Upgrade Power BI Dataflows Gen1 to Dataflow Gen2 (CI/CD) with the Upgrade Wizard and API (Generally Available)

The Dataflows Upgrade Wizard and the Upgrade API for Power BI Dataflows Gen1 to Dataflow Gen2 (CI/CD) are now Generally Available, so you can use them for your production upgrades. The wizard is a guided, end-to-end experience that upgrades a single dataflow, or several dataflows from a workspace, in a single flow. The API lets you assess readiness and upgrade dataflows in bulk, so you can automate upgrades across your workspaces.

New in this release:

  • Upgrade dataflows you don't own: Users with the Admin workspace role and Tenant Admins can now upgrade dataflows owned by others directly in the wizard. The original owner and supported data source connections are kept, so there's no ownership transfer or connection setup to redo.
  • Detect unresolved data source connections: The assessment now flags data source connections that aren't resolved, so you can fix them before you upgrade.
Figure: The assessment flags dataflows with unresolved data source connections before you upgrade.

To learn more, refer to the Upgrade Dataflow Gen1 to Dataflow Gen2 (CI/CD) using the Upgrade Wizard and the Upgrade API documentation.

Mapping Data Flow Transforms in Dataflow Gen2 (Generally Available)

Mapping Data Flow (MDF) Transforms in Dataflow Gen2 can be used for your production transformation workloads in Microsoft Fabric. Build visual, Spark-scale transformations without writing code, or bring existing Mapping Data Flows from Azure Data Factory and Azure Synapse Analytics into Fabric while retaining your transformation logic.

Figure: Visually author and preview Spark-scale transformations with MDF Transforms in Dataflow Gen2.

To learn more, refer to the Mapping Data Flow Transforms in Dataflow Gen2 and the Upgrade Azure Data Factory pipelines with Mapping Data Flows to Fabric documentation.

Bring Viva Insights data to your analytics platform (Preview) 

Copy job and Viva Insights now provide a scheduled, governed way to export Copilot and workplace analytics data into your analytics platform. Organizations measuring the impact of Microsoft 365 Copilot bring adoption and usage data together with HR attributes, license spend, survey results and data from other AI tools, and report on it in the platforms their leadership already uses. Copy job in Microsoft Fabric delivers Viva Insights data to those platforms as a scheduled, fully managed export.  

Figure: The new Viva Insights connector in Copy job.

You choose the Viva Insights datasets you want and the destination they should land in. Microsoft maintains the connector, keeps the schema in step, runs the job on your schedule and recovers failures, so no one on your team must maintain a pipeline. 

For more information, refer to the Viva Insights documentation.

That’s a wrap!

From new data agent capabilities and AI-assisted app development to improvements across data engineering, real-time intelligence, and data preparation, this month’s updates give you more ways to work with your data and turn insights into action.

There will not be a December feature summary, but we’ll be back in the new year with more updates from Microsoft Fabric. Until then, explore the features that are most relevant to your work, refer to the linked documentation to learn more, and let us know what you think.

Check out the Fabric November Monthly Update Video for demos, and more information about this month's updates.
